Madame Defarge. The implacable revolutionary avenger in A Tale of Two Cities who knits coded death lists and presides over the Reign of Terror with cold, methodical vengeance. She knits coded names into patterns at her post in the wine shop, recording the identities of those marked for execution during the French Revolution. She carries a loaded revolver concealed on her person and actively participates in mob violence, including the storming of the Bastille and the massacre of aristocrats. Her vendetta spans decades: her sister was seduced and destroyed by an aristocrat, and she seeks to eliminate his entire lineage in retaliation. She confronts Lucie Manette with threats and coercion, attempting to destroy the family she sees as complicit in her sister's ruin. Her relentless pursuit of justice becomes monstrous; she dies when her own revolver misfires during a struggle with Miss Pross, killed by the very weapon she intended to use as an instrument of vengeance. Dickens shows how personal trauma can corrupt revolutionary ideals into mere cruelty, and how history consumes individuals driven by private grievance. A woman of granite will and historical grievance, she embodies the destructive power of revolution unchecked by mercy.
